Those long in prison sometimes reached passing several amnesties over ten years and still mutually accusing; greatly all were slandered as "non-dao"; upward to the commandant of justice and capital offices, imperial-order prisons arrested reaching sixty or seventy thousand persons; what clerks added was more than a hundred thousand.

Some long-running cases lasted more than ten years and passed through several amnesties while prisoners continued to accuse one another. Nearly all were denounced for conduct contrary to the Way. From the commandant of justice to the capital offices, sixty or seventy thousand people were arrested in cases ordered by the emperor, and clerks added more than a hundred thousand others.
Clarifies that cases lasted more than ten years through several amnesties and distinguishes imperial arrests from clerks' additional implications.

Some inmates rotted there through a dozen general amnesties, denouncing one another until nearly every charge was inflated to "immoral conduct." Cases escalated to the commandant of justice and the capital bureaus until imperial prisons held sixty or seventy thousand souls, and the clerks' own additions swelled the rolls past a hundred thousand.

Some cases dragged on for more than ten years, outlasting several general amnesties as prisoners continued to accuse one another. Nearly every charge was inflated to "conduct contrary to the Way." Cases reaching the commandant of justice and the capital bureaus drew sixty or seventy thousand people into imperial investigations, while clerks implicated more than a hundred thousand others.

At this time the four barbarians were harmonious, within the seas peaceful; Yannian attended to affairs three years, and by old age and illness begged for his bones; the Son of Heaven treated him generously, sent the grand coachman with staff to grant Yannian yellow gold one hundred jin, wine, and in addition sent physicians and drugs; Yannian thereupon claimed illness was grave.

At this time the four quarters were at peace and the realm was tranquil. After Yannian had served for three years, age and illness led him to request retirement. The Son of Heaven treated him generously, sending a Grandee of Palace Splendor with the imperial staff to grant him one hundred jin of gold and wine, together with medicines. Yannian then declared that his illness had become grave.
Corrects 光祿大夫 to Grandee of Palace Splendor and removes physicians not stated in the source.

The frontier was quiet and the realm at peace. After three years in office he cited age and ill health and asked leave to retire. The emperor treated him kindly, sending the grand coachman with a hundred catties of gold, wine, and physicians with medicines. Yannian then insisted his condition was critical.

The frontiers were quiet and the realm at peace. After three years in office, Yannian cited age and illness and asked to retire. The emperor treated him generously, sending a Grandee of Palace Splendor with an imperial staff, one hundred catties of gold, wine, and medicine. Yannian then reported that his condition had become critical.

Tracing the three dynasties' final generations, viewing Zong and Xuan's enjoying the state, examining near kin's omens and verification—disaster and defeat—how was it ever not from women's virtue?

Trace the final generations of the Three Dynasties, consider Gaozong and King Xuan's long possession of their realms, and examine the signs confirmed among more recent kin: when did disaster and ruin not arise from the conduct of women?
Identifies 宗、宣 as Gaozong of Shang and King Xuan of Zhou rather than Han-era rulers or affinal clans.

Trace the last kings of the three ancient dynasties, read how the great affinal clans fared from Emperor Xuan through Emperor Yuan, then look at the omens among your own kin: has catastrophe ever come from anywhere but the inner quarters?

Trace the last generations of the Three Dynasties, consider how long Gaozong of Shang and King Xuan of Zhou enjoyed their realms, and examine the signs confirmed among more recent kin: when did disaster and ruin not turn on the conduct of women?
Identifies 宗、宣 as Gaozong of Shang and King Xuan of Zhou rather than Han-era rulers or affinal clans.

Therefore jade pendants delayed the dawn crowing, Guanju sighs at it, knowing that love of beauty harms nature and shortens years, that departing from the system breeds never satiated—under Heaven will receive transformation, decline and become custom.

Thus the jade pendants sounded late, and the "Guanju" lamented it. It understood that indulgence in beauty injures one's nature and shortens life, while departure from established limits breeds insatiable desire; the realm will absorb that influence until decline becomes custom.
Restores the jade-pendant and Guanju imagery and removes invented ritual bells.

Hence the ritual bells that slowed the morning audience and the sigh of "Guanju" over unchecked passion—excess in the harem wastes the body and shortens life; once the proper numbers are abandoned, desire knows no limit, and the whole realm takes its tone from the palace until decadence becomes habit.

Thus the jade pendants sounded late, and the "Guanju" lamented it. Indulgence in beauty wastes a ruler's vitality and shortens his life; once established limits are abandoned, desire becomes insatiable, and the realm follows the palace until decadence hardens into custom.
Restores the jade-pendant and Guanju imagery and removes invented ritual bells.

Clarifies that the ode seeks a virtuous maiden fit for the ruler.
That is why the classic praises the modest bride who fits her lord: it is the root of loyal service and filial devotion, the very embodiment of humane governance.
That is why the ode celebrates a virtuous maiden fit to be matched with the ruler: it was composed from profound loyalty, filial devotion, and humane concern.
Clarifies that the ode seeks a virtuous maiden fit for the ruler.
King Gaozong of Yin heeded the warning of the crowing pheasants, set his house in order, lived a long life, and restored the dynasty—everything turns on how a ruler answers Heaven.

Gaozong of Shang heeded the warning of the crowing pheasant, corrected himself and set affairs right, enjoyed a lifespan of a hundred years, and restored the Shang way. Everything turns on how a ruler responds to such a warning.
Restores Gaozong's stated hundred-year lifespan and the revival of Shang.

Only may Your Majesty correct empress and secondary consorts, restrain women's favor, guard against extravagance and excess, remove wandering pleasure, personally practice moderation, personally attend to the myriad affairs, frequently ride the secure carriage, by the carriage track, personally attend the two palaces' feasts, extend morning and evening's fixed inquiries.

May Your Majesty set the ranks of empress and consorts in order, restrain favoritism toward women, guard against extravagance, abandon idle excursions, personally practice frugality, attend to the myriad affairs, frequently ride the quiet carriage along the imperial carriageway, personally inspect the meals in the two palaces, and perform the morning and evening inquiries after your elders' health.
Removes unsupported identification of the occupants of the two senior palaces.

Correct the harem hierarchy, curb excessive favor to women, shun luxury and idle sport, practice personal frugality, mind the myriad details of government yourself, ride often in the modest state carriage along the palace carriage ways, attend your mother and aunt in the two palaces in person, and perform the morning and evening courtesies of a filial son.

Set the harem in proper order, curb excessive favoritism, shun luxury and idle excursions, practice frugality, and attend personally to government. Ride often by the palace carriageways to oversee the meals in both senior palaces and perform the morning and evening courtesies owed to your elders.
Removes unsupported identification of the occupants of the two senior palaces.
Confucius said, "Filiality has no beginning or end, yet those who worry they cannot keep pace—there has never been such."

Corrects the filial maxim: failure from beginning to end brings consequences; it is not an endless road metaphor.
Confucius said, "Filial duty is a road without end, yet no one who sets foot on it need ever fear he cannot keep up."
Confucius said, "No one who fails to practice filial duty from beginning to end escapes the consequences."
Corrects the filial maxim: failure from beginning to end brings consequences; it is not an endless road metaphor.

In desiring the empire peace and security and prodigies meaning, none compares to the general; the ruler clearly knows it—therefore he pulls the rope and does not send away; the Documents says Duke do not distress me.

No one desires the realm's peace and an end to the portents more than you, General. The ruler knows this clearly, and so he clings to you and will not let you depart. The Documents says, "Duke, do not leave me in distress!"
Corrects King Cheng's plea to the Duke of Zhou and the direction of the speaker's argument.
No one else can steady the realm or read these omens as you can, and the emperor knows it—hence he clings to you and will not let go. The Documents cry, "My uncle, do not abandon me!"

No one cares more than you for the realm's peace or for ending these portents, and the emperor knows it. That is why he holds on to you and refuses to let you go. In the Documents, King Cheng pleads, "Duke, do not leave me in distress!"
Corrects King Cheng's plea to the Duke of Zhou and the direction of the speaker's argument.

When Hong had earlier been imperial secretary, Fangjin was imperial counselor and recommended the clerk Long as attendant imperial secretary. Hong upheld that Long had earlier deceived on a mission and was unfit to enforce the law in close attendance; Fangjin resented Hong for this.

When Sun Hong had earlier served as Censor-in-Chief, Fangjin was imperial counselor and recommended his clerk Long for appointment as an attendant censor. Hong memorialized that Long had previously deceived the court while on a mission and was unfit to enforce the law in close attendance; Fangjin resented Hong for this.
Restores 奏 and clarifies Sun Hong's objection to Long's appointment.

When Sun Hong had earlier been imperial secretary, Fangjin was imperial counselor and recommended the clerk Long as attendant imperial secretary. Hong upheld that Long had earlier deceived on a mission and was unfit to enforce the law in close attendance; Fangjin resented Hong for this.

When Sun Hong was Censor-in-Chief and Fangjin imperial counselor, Fangjin recommended his clerk Long as an attendant censor. Hong objected in a memorial that Long had deceived the court on an earlier mission and was unfit for a law-enforcement post near the emperor. Fangjin never forgave him.
Restores 奏 and clarifies Sun Hong's objection to Long's appointment.

Marquis of Quyang Gen had earlier assisted government as one of the Three Excellencies. He knew Consort Zhao Feiyi killed the imperial sons yet did not immediately report it; instead he colluded with the Zhao clan, acted willfully and recklessly, slandered the former Empress Xu, imposed wrongful charges, exterminated the Xu clan, and ruined the outer kin of Emperor Yuan.

Marquis of Quyang Wang Gen had earlier assisted the government as one of the Three Excellencies. He knew that Consort Zhao Hede had killed the imperial sons but did not immediately report it; instead he allied himself with the Zhao clan, acted willfully and recklessly, slandered the deposed Empress Xu, imposed false charges on her, destroyed the Xu clan, and ruined Emperor Yuan's maternal family.
Identifies 趙昭儀 as Zhao Hede rather than Zhao Feiyan.

Wang Gen, marquis of Quyang, had earlier assisted government as one of the Three Excellencies. He knew Consort Zhao Feiyi killed the imperial sons yet did not immediately report it; instead he colluded with the Zhao clan, acted willfully and recklessly, slandered the former Empress Xu, imposed wrongful charges, exterminated the Xu clan, and ruined the outer kin of Emperor Yuan.

Wang Gen, marquis of Quyang, had served among the Three Excellencies and helped direct the government. He knew that Consort Zhao Hede had killed the imperial sons but failed to report it. Instead he colluded with the Zhao clan, acted without restraint, slandered the deposed Empress Xu, had her falsely condemned, destroyed the Xu clan, and ruined Emperor Yuan's maternal family.
Identifies 趙昭儀 as Zhao Hede rather than Zhao Feiyan.

Grand Minister of Works Shi Dan and others impeached Dong Hong for misleading the court; Hong was stripped of rank and reduced to commoner status. Du Ye then filed another memorial in his defense.

Grand Minister of Works Shi Dan and the others impeached Dong Hong for misleading the court and acting contrary to the Way. Hong was stripped of rank and reduced to commoner status, but Du Ye submitted another memorial in his defense.
Restores the 不道 charge and makes Du Ye's defense of Dong Hong explicit.
Ye by the situation struck the crack, praised Zhu Bo, destroyed Shi Dan—love-and-hate discussion—can one not fear!
Du Ye took advantage of circumstances to pry at political cracks, praising Zhu Bo and denigrating Shi Dan. Should we not fear arguments governed by personal likes and dislikes?
Clarifies that Du Ye attacked rather than destroyed Shi Dan and sharpens the historian's judgment.
Du Ye exploited every shift in power to drive wedges: he extolled Zhu Bo and ruined Shi Dan. When favor and spite steer memorials at court, the lesson should give us pause.
Du Ye exploited every political opening, praising Zhu Bo and attacking Shi Dan. The danger of letting personal favor and resentment govern public argument should give us pause.
Clarifies that Du Ye attacked rather than destroyed Shi Dan and sharpens the historian's judgment.

At the beginning of Yuandi's reign grain prices soared and refugees filled the roads. When the western Qiang rose in Yongguang, Huan repeatedly donated cash and grain to the treasury—hundreds of thousands over several years.

At the beginning of Emperor Yuan's reign grain prices soared and refugees filled the roads. When the western Qiang rose in Yongguang, Huan repeatedly donated cash and grain to the treasury—several million over the years.
前後數百萬 is several million in aggregate, not hundreds of thousands; 元帝 is Emperor Yuan, so both corrections match the Chinese.

Look at Shi Dan: there was nothing exceptional in his conduct or ability. Xu Shang, Director of the Imperial Clan, was a man disabled by illness. Both obtained high office only because they attached themselves to Fangjin.

Consider Shi Dan: there was nothing exceptional in his conduct or ability. Xu Shang, Superintendent of the Imperial Household, suffered from a disabling illness. Both obtained high office only by attaching themselves to Fangjin.
光祿勳 is Superintendent of the Imperial Household; Director of the Imperial Clan translates 宗正, while the revision avoids an unnecessary parenthetical and demeaning phrasing.

Consider Shi Dan: his conduct and ability were unremarkable, and Director of the Imperial Clan Xu Shang was a man crippled by illness—both gained exalted offices only by attaching themselves to Fangjin.

Consider Shi Dan: his conduct and ability were unremarkable, while Xu Shang, Superintendent of the Imperial Household, suffered from a disabling illness. Both gained exalted offices only by attaching themselves to Fangjin.
The literal likewise misrenders 光祿勳 as Director of the Imperial Clan; the revision uses the established office title and preserves the source's criticism without the draft's harsher wording.
Grand minister of works Shi Dan and others impeached Hong for misleading the court and non-dao; he sat guilty and was dismissed to be commoner; Ye again submitted a memorial suing for Hong.

Grand Minister of Works Shi Dan and the others impeached Dong Hong for misleading the court and acting contrary to the Way. Hong was convicted, dismissed, and reduced to commoner status; Du Ye again submitted a memorial in his defense.
不道 is a charge of acting contrary to the Way, while 訟宏 means defending Dong Hong; restoring the full names also resolves the draft's ambiguous bare references.
